order-ops-basic.why: The order of operations is a shared convention so that one written expression means one thing to everybody. It is not a mathematical truth — it is a grammar. Brackets, then powers, then × and ÷, then + and -.
traps: × and ÷ rank equally and run left to right, and so do + and -. ~8 \div 4 \times 2~ is 4, not 1.

order-ops-nested.why: A fraction bar is a grouping symbol: everything above it is one quantity and everything below is another. That is why ~\f{3+5}{2}~ is 4 and not 3 + 2.5.
traps: When you type a fraction on one line, you must add the brackets the bar was doing for you: ~(3+5)/2~, never ~3+5/2~.

code.body:
(3 + 5) / 2   # 4.0  correct
3 + 5 / 2     # 5.5  the bar's grouping was lost
code.note: Translating a formula into code is where missing brackets become silent wrong answers.

order-ops-traps.why: Almost every order-of-operations error is one of three things: treating equal-rank operations as right-to-left, mishandling a minus sign, or forgetting that ~-x^{2}~ squares only the ~x~.
traps: ~-3^{2} = -9~ but ~(-3)^{2} = 9~. The brackets are the entire difference, and this one appears on every standardised test.
